{"self_assessment": "Impact: I proposed the fish at the start, which gave the table a big, simple animal whose outline reads clearly to a judge. I drew the top fin and the forked tail on the pad, and I laid the upper tail lobe myself (stroke five). The finished picture has a full body, two tail lobes and a fin, and all of it was connected to the start when the push came.

Execution: I kept my hands on the fiddly joins. I traced the tail lobe onto the body line near the tail end, and it carried on from where it stopped instead of being redone. I inspected the fin area closely several times and told Tom exactly which domino was jammed and not catching. After that I kept my hands off the body so nothing got bumped before the push. Before time ran out, the start was tracing through about 122 of 125 standing dominoes.

Collaboration: I split the work early. Maya took the bottom line and the lower tail lobe, Tom took the top line and the fin, and Priya built the body. I took the pad when the body was done so the fin and tail were drawn in one place. I handed out the strokes by number so nobody crowded anyone else, and I kept the instructions short so people could go on building.

Leadership: I set the plan in the first minute, which was animal, facing direction, start position and who takes which line. When Priya put the body on the pad, I adapted and moved on to the fin and tail rather than redrawing it. I kept the table calm and organised through the final minutes, and I called for hands off once everything was connected.

I believe my share of the table's result was about 30 percent. I set the direction and added the fin and tail design, and the rest of the team built the body and fin.", "my_share_percent": 30}
